clue.text: No seat for the " dummy at a wedding rehearsal?

definitions.text: No seat for the " dummy at a wedding rehearsal?

parts.words: No seat for the " dummy at a wedding rehearsal?
parts.note: a stand-in takes the groom's place at a rehearsal, and anyone without a chair is left on their feet

explanation.surface: Someone stands in for the groom at a wedding rehearsal and gets no chair.
explanation.walkthrough: At a rehearsal someone 'stands in' for the absent groom as a dummy, so the place left for them, with no chair, is room to stand.
explanation.definitionFit: Space where an audience must stay on their feet because every chair is taken is what 'no seat' describes.

clue.text: Can these models stand up for their rights ?

definitions.text: Can these models stand up for their rights ?

parts.words: Can these models stand up for their rights ?
parts.note: artist's models who pose seated, so standing up is just what they may not do

explanation.surface: Asking whether fashion models can assert themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand up for their rights' reads as asserting oneself, but literally these models must stay seated.
explanation.definitionFit: People who pose seated for a painter or photographer are models of this kind.

clue.text: They can't help being beastly to one another.

definitions.text: They can't help being beastly to one another.

parts.words: They can't help being beastly to one another.
parts.note: beastly read literally: creatures are by nature beasts to each other

explanation.surface: People who are rude to each other by nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' reads as nasty, but literally means like beasts, which creatures cannot avoid being.
explanation.definitionFit: Creatures of the brute kind are beasts by nature.

clue.text: The proverbial company of musicians

parts.note: the proverb says two's company, so a pair of players is that company

explanation.surface: The well-known band of players.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'two's company' makes a pair the proverbial company; musicians performing in pairs are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Performers of a piece for two voices or instruments work as a pair.

clue.text: They're followed in a straightforward manner.

definitions.text: They're followed in a straightforward manner.

parts.words: They're followed in a straightforward manner.
parts.note: to go straight ahead is to follow the part of your face that sticks out in front

explanation.surface: Instructions obeyed directly.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'follow your nose' means to go straight ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: The facial organs used for smelling are what you follow when going straight on, by the idiom.

clue.text: Free to find a new tenant

explanation.definitionFit: To liberate is to set loose; to let property out again is to rent it once more.

clue.text: Gold coin, oddly enough, and a ring found in a river

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry

indicators.note: oddly says the letters of the word just before it are set out strangely

parts.note: O is round like a ring

explanation.surface: A gold coin and a ring are discovered in a riverbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly enough' rearranges COIN to INOC.
explanation.definitionFit: A major South American waterway flows through Venezuela.

clue.text: He cannot handle clients who lose their heads

definitions.text: He cannot handle clients who lose their heads

parts.words: He cannot handle clients who lose their heads
parts.note: a practitioner who reads character from the bumps of the skull needs clients with heads to feel

explanation.surface: A professional unable to cope with panicking customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose their heads' reads as panic, but literally a headless client leaves this skull-reader nothing to handle.
explanation.definitionFit: A practitioner of the old pseudoscience of reading the skull's bumps studies heads.

clue.text: One of an ancient race of sloggers ?

definitions.text: One of an ancient race of sloggers ?

parts.words: One of an ancient race of sloggers ?
parts.note: an ancient people of Anatolia, read as if the name meant a tribe of big hitters

explanation.surface: A question about an old tribe famous for hitting hard.
explanation.walkthrough: A slogger is someone who hits hard, a 'hitter'; the name of the Bronze Age people of Anatolia begins with that word.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Anatolian people with an empire around 1600-1200 BC are a race from antiquity.

clue.text: Anger makes a sailor cross.

parts.note: an old salt is a seasoned sailor
ire is an old word for anger

explanation.surface: Losing his temper puts a seaman in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective (angry) but is the noun: the diagonal cross of St Andrew on the Scottish flag.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagonal X-shaped cross in heraldry is called by this name.

clue.text: They help one to land

parts.note: people who help a buyer acquire property, read as if guiding an aircraft down

explanation.surface: Describing air-traffic controllers or similar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To land' reads as touching down, but means to obtain land and houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Firms that sell property for clients help buyers secure houses.

clue.text: Refined and with a gentle disposition

indicators.note: disposition here means arrangement, so the letters of the words before it are set out afresh

explanation.surface: Describing someone cultured and of mild temperament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposition' reads as temperament but signals rearranging A GENTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Graceful and stylish in manner is the sense of refined here.

clue.text: Maybe a poster could bring in trade

indicators.note: maybe says the letters of the words after it are only one possible arrangement

explanation.surface: Advertising with a placard might attract customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' signals rearranging A POSTER; the definition describes what a harbour town does for commerce.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour town where ships unload goods is a place that brings commerce in.

clue.text: A date no doubt at this filling station ?

definitions.text: A date no doubt at this filling station ?

parts.words: A date no doubt at this filling station ?
parts.note: a desert watering place where date palms grow and travellers refill with water

explanation.surface: A romantic meeting at a petrol station.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'date' is the fruit of the palm, not a rendezvous, and the 'filling station' is where caravans take on water in the desert.
explanation.definitionFit: A fertile spot in the desert with water and palms is where travellers replenish supplies.

clue.text: On board the ' Arethusa "?

parts.note: the old sea song calls the ship the saucy Arethusa, so she is a saucy vessel

explanation.surface: A question about life aboard a famous sailing ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Saucy Arethusa' is an old British sea song about a frigate, so the ship is a 'saucy boat'; the answer is the jug gravy is served in at table.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat-shaped jug for gravy or sauce at the dinner table has this name.

clue.text: Stress the importance of the Tube ?

explanation.definitionFit: To emphasise something is to mark it with a stroke beneath; London's underground railway is a line that runs below.

clue.text: Work is forced when under a tyrant's thumb

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
pressed means forced or compelled

explanation.surface: Labour is compulsory under a dictatorship.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone kept down by harsh rule is subjugated by a despot.

clue.text: Nationality of a sniper, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the words before it may be put in another order

explanation.surface: Asking where a marksman comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: An Iranian, a native of the old empire of Persia, has this nationality.

clue.text: Was an illustration at one time quite enough?

parts.note: ex means former, at one time
ample means plentiful, quite enough

explanation.surface: Asking whether a picture was once sufficient.
explanation.definitionFit: A case that illustrates a point is a specimen or instance.

clue.text: Not the first rays, literally

parts.note: a type of radiation named with a Greek letter that is not the opening one of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Not the earliest sunlight of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: Radiation types are named alpha, beta and gamma; 'literally' points to the letters: this ray is named after the third Greek letter, not the first (alpha).
explanation.definitionFit: High-energy radiation is named after the third letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Vet cavorts with goat in the dance

indicators.note: cavorts means prances about, so the letters of the words around it jump into a new order

explanation.surface: An animal doctor frolics with a goat at a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: An old French court dance in moderate four-time is a stately measure.

clue.text: The Archers' large war reserve of vegetables

definitions.text: The Archers' large war reserve of vegetables

parts.words: The Archers' large war reserve of vegetables
parts.note: archers keep arrows for war, and a large supply would be 'more arrows', said quickly a kind of big squash

explanation.surface: A reference to a farming radio drama's wartime stock of produce.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archers is a long-running BBC radio farming soap; archers stock arrows, and 'more arrows' run together sounds like these large vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: Large green gourds of the squash family are garden vegetables.

clue.text: Not a way-out form of hostilities

definitions.text: Not a way-out form of hostilities

parts.words: Not a way-out form of hostilities
parts.note: routes leading in rather than out, also the word for advances made by an attacking force

explanation.surface: A conventional rather than eccentric kind of fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way-out' looks like 'eccentric' but means roads leading out; the opposite, roads leading in, gives the word for hostile incursions.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostile advances into enemy territory are incursions made by an invading force.

clue.text: A good man and a dissolute one take off together

parts.note: St, saint, is a good man
a rip is an old word for a rake or dissolute person

explanation.surface: A saint and a rake undress side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: RIP is an old word for a dissolute fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: To undress or remove clothes is to remove them.

clue.text: How the favourites get into step

definitions.text: How the favourites get into step

parts.words: How the favourites get into step
parts.note: favourites are pets, and the four letters of pets read backwards make step

explanation.surface: How the leading contenders fall into line.
explanation.walkthrough: Favourites are 'pets'; written backwards they spell 'step', so turning them round is how they become step.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning a word back to front is the process that changes one into the other.

clue.text: No sure-footed excursionist

definitions.meaning: one who stumbles is no sure-footed walker
someone on a day out or outing

explanation.definitionFit: One who stumbles is not steady on their feet, and a day visitor on an outing is also called this.

clue.text: Anthem for a foreign king entering in a race

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: entering says one piece goes inside the others here

parts.note: TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
roi is French for king

explanation.surface: A national song for an overseas monarch competing in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A race' is the Isle of Man TT motorcycle race; 'entering' signals the French king going inside, and the definition is the opening chant of the Mass, not a national anthem.
explanation.definitionFit: The psalm or chant sung at the start of Mass is a sacred song.

clue.text: They are certainly not tongue-tied

parts.note: people whose job is putting one language into another are anything but lost for words in foreign tongues

explanation.surface: Describing fluent, talkative people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' means language: these people work freely across languages.
explanation.definitionFit: Translators of speech between languages are fluent in more than one tongue.
